clue.text: Hack introduced foreign poetry — how cliched!

indicators.note: foreign suggests something strange and unfamiliar, so the letters are made unfamiliar by rearranging them
the horse word has something introduced into it, so it wraps around the other piece

parts.note: a hack is a horse for ordinary riding, as is a steed
the letters of poetry rearranged

explanation.surface: A journalist brings foreign verse into a piece and a critic sneers at how hackneyed it is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hack' looks like a journalist, but here it is a riding horse; the rearranged poetry sits inside STE-ED.
explanation.definitionFit: Something stereotyped is formulaic and unoriginal, the same idea as a cliched expression, here an exclamation turned adjective.

clue.text: Health professional makes statement on the sex offender

parts.note: a speech is a formal statement
the article taken as written; on places it after the first piece
a rapist commits a sexual offence

explanation.surface: A news report about a clinician who issues a statement concerning a criminal.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface breaks the answer at the wrong point: THERAPIST hides THE + RAPIST.
explanation.definitionFit: A speech therapist is a clinician who treats difficulties with talking, so is one kind of health professional.

clue.text: Shame at having run away, leaving one with bill

indicators.note: something that has run away is no longer there, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: a shame, as in 'it is a shame', is a matter for regret
R is the cricket abbreviation for a run

explanation.surface: Someone ashamed of fleeing a restaurant is left holding the bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a restaurant tab, but it is a beak; take R out of REGRET.
explanation.definitionFit: An egret is a heron-like wading bird, and every bird has a bill, so it is one with a beak.

clue.text: The final gesture shows feeling

indicators.note: final points to the very end of the word before it, so only its closing letter is kept

parts.note: the last letter of The
a motion of the hand is a gesture

explanation.surface: A farewell wave reveals what someone really feels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The final gesture' reads as one phrase, a last wave; split it into the last letter of The and a gesture.
explanation.definitionFit: Emotion is a synonym for feeling, as in a strong mental state such as joy or grief.

clue.text: Most ran off to find bar

indicators.note: off means gone bad or wrong, so these letters are in the wrong order and must be rearranged

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Most of the crowd ran off to find a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' suggests a pub at the end of the run; it is a structural beam.
explanation.definitionFit: A transom is a horizontal crossbar in a window or above a door, so it is a structural bar.

clue.text: Reportedly did well in exam about the countryside

indicators.note: reportedly means as said by others, so the phrase is taken by its sound rather than spelling

parts.note: to pass an oral is to do well in a spoken exam

explanation.surface: A rumour that someone did well in a geography test on rural life.
explanation.walkthrough: An oral is a spoken examination; 'passed oral' run together gives the sound of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Pastoral means relating to rural life, shepherds and farmland, so it describes things concerning the countryside.

clue.text: Double a racy wager drunkenly, including one for the road

parts.note: dual means double, twofold

indicators.note: including means taking in, so the letters for one are put among the others
drunkenly suggests staggering about out of order, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A tipsy gambler doubles a risky bet and orders one more drink for the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One for the road' is a last drink before leaving; here 'one' is I and 'road' alone is the definition. A dual carriageway is a British divided highway.
explanation.definitionFit: A dual carriageway is a British highway with a central reservation dividing two lanes of traffic, so it is a kind of road.

clue.text: That's caught in cover for very cold place

indicators.note: in tells us one piece sits inside the other, here the caught letter goes within the phrase for that is

parts.note: i.e. stands for id est, that is
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
a cap is a covering, as for the head or a bottle

explanation.surface: Someone trapped under shelter in a freezing spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's' stands for i.e., id est, Latin for that is; the caught letter sits inside it before the cover follows.
explanation.definitionFit: An icecap is a permanent dome of ice covering polar land, so it is an extremely frigid location.

clue.text: Son upset and embarrassed, sounded asleep

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and disordered, so the letters of the word before are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of Son rearranged
an embarrassed face goes red

explanation.surface: A boy is upset and mortified because he dozed off and was heard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' seems to describe the son's mood, but it shuffles his letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To snore is to breathe noisily during sleep, so a snoring person sounded asleep.

clue.text: This may be my final word

definitions.text: This may be my final word

parts.words: This may be my final word
parts.note: surface reading: a last pronouncement, perhaps a dying utterance or ultimatum
setter's reading: the word said on leaving, a casual British goodbye

explanation.walkthrough: 'Final word' suggests a solemn last statement; the joke is it is just the cheery word you say when departing.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheerio is an informal British farewell, said as the last thing when parting company.

clue.text: Don't get involved in slur on a head boy

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: head is the top or front of something, so only the first letter of the following word is used

parts.note: the first letter of boy
a slur on someone's name is a stain on it

explanation.surface: Advice to keep out of a smear campaign against the head boy of a school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slur on' means the slur comes after A and B; 'head boy' looks like a school prefect, but only gives the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To abstain is to refrain from taking part, as in a vote, which is choosing not to get involved.

clue.text: Drinks firm lacks IT engineer

indicators.note: to engineer is to construct or rework, so the preceding letters are rebuilt in a new order

parts.note: Co. is the abbreviation for company, a firm
the letters of lacks and IT rearranged

explanation.surface: A company has no computer technician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Engineer' looks like the job the firm needs filled, but it is a verb telling you to rework the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Cocktails are mixed alcoholic beverages, so they are a type of drink, the plural matching the plural definition.

clue.text: Result of our accepting a quantity

indicators.note: accepting means taking in, so the first word receives the other piece inside it

parts.note: taken as written
cc, a cubic centimetre, is a quantity of liquid

explanation.surface: An outcome of us taking on a certain amount.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Result' looks like a noun but is the verb meaning come about.
explanation.definitionFit: To result, used as a verb, means to happen as a consequence, so it can mean to occur.

clue.text: Course apt to change by an hour

indicators.note: to change means to alter, so the letters of the word before are put in a different order

parts.note: the letters of apt rearranged
h is the abbreviation for hour

explanation.surface: A route that is likely to alter within the hour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Course' could be a meal or a class; here it is a route.
explanation.definitionFit: A path is a route or track followed, which is what a course of travel is.

clue.text: Whole university confronts politician before broadcast

parts.note: uni is the short form of university
an MP is a Member of Parliament
a programme that has been broadcast has been aired

explanation.surface: A whole university challenges an MP ahead of a televised debate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confronts' and 'before' only place the pieces side by side in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Unimpaired means undamaged and intact, so it describes something whole and in full working order.

clue.text: Living companion met with fatal complication

indicators.note: a complication tangles things up, so the letters before it are twisted into a new order

parts.note: the fodder of met and fatal; with only joins them

explanation.surface: A partner at home suffered a deadly medical setback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Living' sounds like alive as opposed to fatal, but means sharing living space. In Britain a flat is an apartment.
explanation.definitionFit: A flatmate is someone who shares an apartment with you, a companion in the place you live.

clue.text: Time limit on computer program

parts.note: a spell is a period of time
to check is to restrain or limit

explanation.surface: A deadline imposed on software.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time limit' reads as one phrase, but is two pieces: a spell and a check.
explanation.definitionFit: A spellcheck is software that finds misspelt words in a document, so it is a computer program.

clue.text: Form of transport from southern lake to border

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for southern
L is the abbreviation for lake on maps
an edge is a border

explanation.surface: A vehicle that travels from a lake in the south up to the frontier.
explanation.definitionFit: A sledge is a vehicle on runners for sliding over snow, so it is one means of getting about.

clue.text: Most current greeting uttered very quietly at outset

indicators.note: out can mean out of order or wrong, so the letters of the next word are rearranged

parts.note: hi is an informal greeting
pp, pianissimo, is the musical marking for very quietly
split as out and set: the letters of set rearranged, with out signalling the shuffle

explanation.surface: The most up-to-date hello is whispered at the start of a meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outset' must be split: out signals the shuffle and set is what gets shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Hip means fashionable and up to date, so the hippest thing is the most fashionable and current.

clue.text: Reminder to bring in variety pack as teatime treat

indicators.note: variety implies a mixed assortment, so the letters following are mixed up
to bring in is to take something inside, so the prompt word surrounds the other letters

parts.note: a cue is a prompt or reminder, as to an actor
the letters of pack rearranged

explanation.surface: A note to remember to bring an assortment box for afternoon tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Variety pack' reads as a mixed box of goods, but variety only signals the jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: A cupcake is a small iced sponge cake, the sort of sweet thing served at afternoon tea.

clue.text: Disability has some overall impact

indicators.note: has some says only a portion of the following words is used, a run of consecutive letters

parts.note: a run of letters across the two words

explanation.surface: A statement that a handicap has a partial effect on everything.
explanation.definitionFit: A limp is an uneven walk caused by an injured or disabled leg, so it is a physical disability.

clue.text: Setback for chap with a hit show

indicators.note: a setback sets things back, so the following pieces are read from end to start

parts.note: Ed is a man's name, any chap
taken as written
a rap is a sharp blow

explanation.surface: A man suffers a reversal even though his show was a success.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A hit show' reads as a popular production, but hit is a blow and show alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A parade is a public procession or display, and to parade something is to show it off.

clue.text: Play points to sham

parts.note: E and N are compass points, east and north
putting on an act is a sham or pretence

explanation.surface: A drama that indicates fakery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play' looks like a noun, a drama, but is the verb meaning to act out.
explanation.definitionFit: To enact is to act out or perform a role or scene, which is to play it.

clue.text: Performer goes home with man on the rebound

parts.note: to pop is to go somewhere briefly, as in pop round
someone who is home is in

indicators.note: something on the rebound bounces back the way it came, so the man's name is read backwards

parts.note: Reg is a man's name

explanation.surface: A celebrity heads home with a new man straight after a break-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the rebound' suggests a romance after a split; it only turns the man's name round.
explanation.definitionFit: A pop singer is a vocalist in popular music, so is one kind of performer.

clue.text: Did little with credentials presented by student journalist

parts.note: ID, identification, is a person's credentials
L is for learner, as on a British learner driver's plate
ed. is short for editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: A lazy trainee reporter flashes a press pass and does no work.
explanation.definitionFit: To idle is to spend time doing nothing much, so someone who idled was inactive.

clue.text: Bitter-sweet expression

parts.note: grim means harsh and bitter
sweet as slang approval means great, ace

explanation.surface: A face showing mixed feelings, at once sad and happy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bitter-sweet' looks like one word; the hyphen hides two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A grimace is a twisted facial expression of pain or disgust, so it is one kind of expression on the face.

clue.text: Conceded everyone was in debt

parts.note: all means everyone
someone in debt owed money

explanation.surface: An admission that the whole group owed money.
explanation.definitionFit: Allowed, in the sense of admitted or granted, is a synonym of conceded, as in 'he allowed that I was right'.

clue.text: Recently he hated Tory spin

indicators.note: spin turns things round and round, so the letters before it are thrown into a new order

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Not long ago a man said he hated Conservative party propaganda.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spin' looks like political news management, which fits Tory; here it is the shuffle signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The other day is an idiom for a short while ago, an informal way of saying recently.
